The graph of the first derivative $y={f}^{′}(x)$ of the function $f(x)$ intersects the $x$-axis at the points $x=-6,$ $x=-1,$ and $x=3,$ as shown above. Find all the values of $x$ where the function $y=f(x)$ is increasing.

$x\in (-\infty ,$
{{field-1}}$)⋃($
{{field-2}}$,$
{{field-3}}$)$
question.worked_solution:
First, we recall the following:

- If ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ for all $x\in (a,b),$ then the slope of $f(x)$ is equal to zero on $(a,b).$

- If ${f}^{′}(x)>0$ for all $x\in (a,b),$ then the slope of $f(x)$ is positive on $(a,b).$

- If ${f}^{′}(x)<0$ for all $x\in (a,b),$ then the slope of $f(x)$ is negative on $(a,b).$

From the above graph, we can see that ${f}^{′}(x)$ is positive on the intervals $(-\infty ,-6)$ and $(-1,3):$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14193353/assets/4b8010c256447c91b20c0b1c3d2099d7b6739aca5c32ddb4fed357c4a3376759.png)

Therefore, $f(x)$ is increasing when

$$
x\in (-\infty ,-6\,)⋃(\,-1,3\,).
$$
